data.copy:
I will NEVER trim my cat's nails again.

Not because I don't care if she gets ingrown claws.

But because I found a way to keep her nails perfectly short without ever picking up a pair of clippers, wrapping her in a towel, or driving her to the groomer.

She does it herself.

In 30 seconds. While she plays.

And I haven't touched her paws in seven months.

I'm 68 years old. My hands aren't what they used to be. I can't get down on the floor like I used to. And I sure as hell can't hold a seven-pound demon down while she screams bloody murder.

I spent two years trying.

Two years of the burrito wrap. The grinder. The cone. The bag. The towel over her face.

Two years of my husband bleeding while she wriggled free.

Two years of being at my wits end and ending each session with maybe ONE nail trimmed.

If I was lucky.

She has 18.

Do the math.

If you've been at war with your cat over her nails like I was, you need to hear this.

---

Three weeks after I finally gave up trying, Mittens started licking her front paw obsessively.

Then she started limping.

I picked her up and looked at her paw.

One of her claws had grown so long it had curved completely around and punctured her paw pad.

Swollen. Red. Oozing yellow-green discharge.

I felt so stupid. In hindsight, I should have checked it.

I called my son crying.

"My cat is going to die."

He drove 90 minutes to my house, picked us up, and took us to the emergency vet.

$640 later, we had a diagnosis.

Infected ingrown claw. Sedation to remove it. Antibiotics. A cone of shame for ten days.

The vet pulled me aside before we left.

"This is one of the most common emergency visits we see in indoor cats. Owners stop trimming because it's too hard. The nails curl into the pad. The pad gets infected. We end up sedating the cat and removing the claw surgically. It's painful, expensive, and completely preventable."

I sat in the passenger seat on the ride home.

Holding the carrier on my lap.

Completely silent.

I want to ask you a question before I tell you this story.

When was the last time you got a good morning text from your best friend.

Mine used to come every single day at 6:42 AM. Sometimes 6:43. Sometimes 6:38 if she was up early with her dog. It was always something dumb. A coffee emoji. A picture of the sunrise from her kitchen window. The word "Monday" with three eye roll emojis. For 22 years that text was as much a part of my morning as my coffee.

I sat at my kitchen table on a Sunday in October and I scrolled back through our message thread and I realized the last good morning text I'd gotten from her was August 14th.

It was October 26th.

That's 73 days. 73 mornings. And I hadn't noticed.

I want you to read this whole thing because what I figured out about my best friend, and what I figured out about myself in the process, is something I think is happening to a lot of women our age and nobody is naming it. We're disappearing one quiet morning at a time and the people who love us aren't noticing because we're disappearing too slowly to register.

Until something cracks.

"I've been a diabetic for nine years. I did everything right. My shoulder broke down anyway."

That was the first line of a post I read at 2:47am.

I was in a women's health group I'd found by accident. On my phone in the dark.

Pillow wedged under my right elbow. Couldn't sleep. Again.

I screenshot the post before I read the second line. Because the first line was already my life and I needed to make sure I didn't lose it.

If you're a diabetic woman somewhere between 45 and 65.

And your shoulder has been doing something not right for longer than you want to admit.

And you've spent years being "the good diabetic."

Checking. Walking. Smaller plates.

Saying no to dessert at every family dinner for a decade.

And you've tried the physical therapy and the cortisone and the supplements and maybe a specialist or two for the shoulder.

And every single one of them only looked at the joint. Or only looked at your blood sugar.

And nothing got better.

This post is for you.

I want to tell you something nobody in any of those exam rooms told me.

My name doesn't matter. What matters is this.

I'm 57. I've been diabetic since I was 48.

I have a callus on the side of my left index finger from nine years of finger pricks.

There's a sensor patch on the back of my arm.

I've worn one for so long my husband says he forgets it's not just part of my skin.

I haven't eaten bread at a restaurant since my daughter's college graduation. That was 2017.

The cabinet next to the coffee maker has my metformin, a backup glucose meter, the extra sensors, and the little notebook where I used to write everything down before the CGM came in.

My husband knows my numbers.

This is what I've been doing for nine years.

Every single day. Without taking a break.

Il y a 2 ans, tout le monde pensait que j'en avais 35.
Puis quelque chose s'est produit entre mes 44 et 45 ans. Quelque chose de violent que personne n'ose vraiment dire tout haut.
Mon visage a littéralement fondu.
Pas progressivement. Pas "oh, une petite ride par-ci par-là."
Non.
Du jour au lendemain.

Septembre 2023.
Je me réveille. Je vais dans la salle de bain. Je me regarde dans le miroir.

Je me suis assise sur le rebord de la baignoire.
Et j'ai pleuré.
Parce que ce n'était pas juste "vieillir normalement."
C'était comme si mon visage avait vieilli de 10 ans en 6 mois.

data.copy:
My Cat Slept on the End of My Bed Every Night for Eleven Years. Last Winter, She Started Sleeping on the Floor. Here's What Brought Her Back Up.

I want to tell you about my cat.

Her name is Millie.

She's thirteen.

We got her from a shelter in the winter of 2013, the year my youngest started high school. She was the small tabby at the back of the pen who didn't come to the front. The volunteer told us she'd been passed over twice.

We took her home that afternoon.

For eleven years, Millie slept on the end of my bed.

Every single night, the same routine. I'd turn off the lamp. I'd hear her come down the hallway. There'd be a pause at the door — a couple of seconds, like she was measuring — then the run-up, then the jump, then the thump of her landing near my feet.

Then three slow turns, and she'd settle against my ankles.

Eleven years. My husband travelled a lot for work in those years. There were plenty of nights when that thump was the last sound of my day, and I stopped being able to fall asleep properly without it.

You don't think of something like that as a ritual while it's happening.

You think of it as just what the cat does.

Last winter, the thump stopped.

The first night, I assumed she was sulking somewhere. Cats do that.

In the morning I found her asleep on the folded blanket on the floor beside my side of the bed.

I told myself she was too warm. It happens.

But it wasn't one night. It was the next night, and the one after that. By August she had a permanent spot on the floor blanket, and I had rearranged my own story about it. She prefers it down there. It's her new spot. Cats change their minds.

Cats do change their minds.

That wasn't what this was.

Because once I was honest about the bed, I started noticing the other things.

She wasn't on the kitchen bench in the mornings anymore, supervising the kettle. That had been a fixture of my life for a decade and I genuinely could not tell you when it stopped.

She'd stopped following me up…

I'm a Cardiologist. And I Need to Tell You Why 23 of My Patients Who Were Taking Nattokinase Came Back With the Exact Same Blood Pressure Numbers After 90 Days. What I Discovered Changed How I Practice Medicine.

My name is Dr. Michael Harrison. I've been practicing cardiology for 25 years.

Three years ago, something started happening in my office that I couldn't explain.

Patients were coming in with blood pressure supplements they'd found online. Not the usual garbage — not the $12 garlic pills from Walmart or the celebrity-endorsed nonsense from TV.

These patients had done real research. They'd found nattokinase on Reddit, on longevity podcasts, on biohacker forums. They'd read about the fibrinolytic properties. They understood the mechanism — or thought they did.

And I was genuinely impressed. These weren't desperate people grabbing anything off the shelf. These were educated, analytical people who'd done more homework than most of my colleagues.

So when they told me they were taking nattokinase for their blood pressure, I didn't object. The research exists. The enzyme breaks down fibrin. It has legitimate science behind it.

I told them to track their numbers and come back in 90 days.

That's when the pattern started.

The first patient — let's call him Daniel — came back at the 90-day mark. Fifty-six years old. Software engineer. Meticulous tracker. Had a spreadsheet of twice-daily readings going back twelve weeks.

"Doc, look at this," he said, sliding his laptop across my desk.

Week 1 through 3: his blood pressure dropped from 151/96 to 142/89. Steady decline. Exactly what you'd expect if the nattokinase was working.

Week 4: 140/88. Still improving.

Week 8: 139/87.

Week 9: 140/88.

Week 10: 141/89.

Week 12: 141/88.

data.copy:
I found a photo of myself from 3 years ago.

My sister tagged me in it on Facebook.

I didn't recognize the woman in it.

She had hair down to her chest.

So thick she complained about it taking forever to dry.

So full that ponytails gave her headaches from the weight.

The kind of hair I used to resent because it was "too much."

I would give anything to have that problem now.

I turned off my phone and caught my reflection in the black screen.

Thin. See-through. Scalp showing pink through the part.

I counted the strands I could see at my hairline.

23.

I used to not be able to see individual strands.

Now I could count them like blades of grass.

I sat there staring at myself for a full minute.

Then I started crying and couldn't stop.

========

The showers are the worst part.

I started showering in the dark.

Because seeing it fall was worse than feeling it.

I would stand outside the tub shaking before turning on the water.

Negotiating with God.

"Please. Just one normal shower. Just one."

But nothing prepared me for the feeling of it coming out.

Not from brushing.

Not from pulling.

From just... touching it.

Like pulling apart wet cotton candy.

Clumps in my hands every single time.

I would make sounds I didn't know I could make.

Grateful the water drowned out my sobbing.

Grateful no one could see me like that.

========

The drain became my enemy.

Had to snake it twice a week.

The landlord sent maintenance.

He looked at the hair I pulled out and said, "You got a dog?"

"No," I said. "It's mine."

He looked at my head. Looked back at the drain snake.

Said nothing.

I wanted to die from embarrassment.

========

I started finding hair everywhere.

My keyboard at work.

My coffee mug.

My pillow every morning.

My manager moved our weekly meeting to her office.

She didn't say why.

But I knew.

Nobody wants to sit in a chair covered in someone else's hair.

I started bringing a lint roller to work.

Rolling my chair before anyone came in.

My wife and I have been married for thirty-six years.

For about three of them, I had been slowly disappearing on her.

And I had not had the courage to tell her so.

I'm sixty-two years old.

We met at the community college where she was studying to be a dental hygienist and I was finishing my certification in plumbing, and we got married sixteen months later, which is something neither of us recommends to our children.

It worked out for us. It mostly doesn't.

The disappearing I'm talking about did not happen all at once.

It almost never does.

It happened the way these things happen — in small pieces over a long time, none of which I noticed individually, all of which I could see clearly when I finally turned around and looked at the three years behind me.

I had been less present at the dinner table.

Less interested in the small things Donna wanted to tell me about her day.

Less inclined to suggest the small Saturday-afternoon outings we used to take — the drive to the farm stand, the bookshop in Kutztown, the diner near the reservoir.

I had been falling asleep in my chair earlier in the evening.

Quieter on long drives where we used to talk for hours.

I had been, in ways I could feel but not put a name to, a smaller version of the man I had been for the first thirty-three years of our marriage.

I had also been telling myself it was normal.

I told myself it was age. I told myself it was the stress at the plumbing company, the weight of the responsibilities I had taken on there that did not go away when I got home in the evening.

I told myself it was the sleep that wasn't as good as it used to be, and the back that ached in the morning the way it didn't when I was forty-five, and the long winter we'd had two years running.

And I told myself, in the part of my mind I do not usually visit, that it was something else too.

Something I did not want to look at directly.

Something I had been carrying quietly for two or three years and had not said to any…

data.caption: The VA never told you this.
data.copy:
The ringing doesn't scare me anymore.The quiet does. It took me eleven years to figure out why — and why everything I tried couldn't change it.

I used to come home from noise.

Flight line. Engines. Range days. Machinery.

The kind of noise you feel in your teeth.

Now I turn noise on just to survive the quiet.

Fan at night.

TV low in the background.

Rain sounds from my phone.

A podcast I'm not even listening to.

Anything to keep the room from going dead silent.

Because when the room goes quiet, the ringing steps forward.

Not louder exactly.

Bigger.

Like it was waiting for everything else to shut up.

My wife used to ask why the TV was still on.

I'd say, "I sleep better with background noise."

Clean lie.

Easy lie.

The kind nobody questions.

Because it sounds normal.

Except I wasn't relaxing.

I was defending myself from silence.

There's a difference.

And the worst part is how normal I'd made it.

That was my life. Not treatment. Not healing. A system. A sad little operating procedure for getting through the night.

And the worst part? I was proud of it. Because that's what I do. I adapt. I figure things out. I find a way.

Except this wasn't a solution.

It was me building my whole life around the one thing I couldn't fix.

So I went to the VA. Sat in the chair. And got told what a lot of veterans get told.

Tinnitus. Ten percent. Permanent. Manage it.

That was the whole plan.

Manage it.

Like I hadn't already built my entire life around managing it.

Like the fan, the TV, the rain sounds, the jaw clenching, and the 1 AM Googling were just hobbies.

They gave me hearing aids.

They helped some.

Restaurants got easier.

Conversations got clearer.

I stopped nodding along and hoping nobody asked me a question I hadn't heard.

So yeah, they helped.

But then night came.

I took them out.

The house got quiet.

And the ringing was still there.

Same sound. Same place. Waiting.

So I tried the rest.

White noise. Masking. CBT. Magnesium. Zinc. Gink…

keyword.description: Free-text search string (lowercased server-side). Use for product names, brands, hooks, domains — not for category/niche (use niches).
keyword.allowed_values: Any string; empty = no text filter.

searchkeyword.description: Which ad field keyword searches. NOT a niche/category selector.
searchkeyword.allowed_values: All, landingurl, pagename, adtext, productname. Default All when keyword is set.

countries.description: Ad target countries (where the ad runs — wlads.countries). Not store HQ.
countries.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated ISO2: US, GB, DK, NL, BE, IE, NO, SE, FR, DE, IT, CA, NZ, AU, BR, AT, CH, ES, FI, PL, PT, GR, TR, AE, SA, QA, KW, BH, OM, JO, IL, LB, IQ, EG.
countries.notes: MX/CO/CL are not in this Meta targeting catalog. Use store_based_in for stores based in those markets.

excludeCountries.allowed_values: Comma-separated ISO2: US, GB, DK, NL, BE, IE, NO, SE, FR, DE, IT, CA, NZ, AU, BR, AT, CH, ES, FI, PL, PT, GR, TR, AE, SA, QA, KW, BH, OM, JO, IL, LB, IQ, EG.

storebasedin.description: Store Based In (dashboard storebasedin → store_traffic.shop_origin_country). Use for Mexico/Colombia/Chile/etc. store HQ.
storebasedin.allowed_values: Comma-separated ISO2 including MX, CO, CL, AR, PE and other Explore Shops Based In markets.

niches.description: Product category / vertical filter (dashboard Meta niches). Use when user asks for a category, niche, vertical, or market — not keyword.
niches.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated codes: CG, AM, GG, JY, GS, HT, BY, BG, SK, WC, MC, SP, KS, TS, HE, PS, DP, HI, FT, OG, OP, TR, AC, AA, BM, FK, SH, SW, EL, FW, WT, EW, FR, GM, PH, EC, WE, SC, BE, MU, PA, CB, CF, CP, DC, CT, HH, SG, YG, CC, PZ, LS, GP, WN, SF, OR, MG, PB. See allowed_niches in response for code→label map. Fashion/clothing = CG.

website.description: Detected store/checkout technology on the landing page (dashboard Website filter).
website.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated codes: SH, TP, BU, LS, CC, SL, TA, GG, FU, CS, LP, FO, SI, GP, XS, YC, HY, DI, MS, SB, PP, WC, TT, TW, PI, GO, SC, FB, MG, WP, SQ, PS, GM, KV, CO, HJ, WX, AR, BC, MC. SH=Shopify, WC=WooCommerce, CS=Clickfunnels. See allowed_technologies in response.

languages.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated: en, nl, de, no, fr, sv, da, it, pt, es, fi, pl, tr, ar, he.

excludeLanguages.allowed_values: Comma-separated: en, nl, de, no, fr, sv, da, it, pt, es, fi, pl, tr, ar, he.

apps.description: Shopify apps detected on the store.
apps.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated app names/ids from dashboard Apps filter. See allowed_apps in response.

excludeApps.description: Exclude stores using these Shopify apps.
excludeApps.allowed_values: Comma-separated app names/ids. See allowed_apps in response.

themes.description: Shopify theme name on the store (exact match).
themes.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated exact theme names from dashboard Themes filter (discover via GET /api/themes).

scaling.allowed_values: rising, stable, declining, nodownscaling, upscaling, downscaling.

mediafilter.allowed_values: videos, images, carousel, dco. Omit/All = all formats.

pagetypefilter.allowed_values: products, collections, funnels, nofunnels. Empty/All = all types.

adscorefilter.description: WinningHunter ad score tier (Established / Has Potential / Unestablished).
adscorefilter.allowed_values: winning (Established), scaling (Has Potential), testing (Unestablished). Requires matching account tier.

lowimpressions.description: Hide ads with very low impressions.
lowimpressions.allowed_values: hide (exclude low-impression rows). Omit = show all.

rankgrowthfilter.description: Within-brand ad rank momentum vs historic rank_history.
rankgrowthfilter.allowed_values: Comma-separated subset of: rising, stable, declining.

minadrank.description: Minimum within-brand ad rank (lower rank number = stronger ad for that brand, e.g. #1).

min.description: Minimum duplicate/active-seen ad count on the page.

minactiveads.description: Minimum active Meta ads on the advertiser Facebook page (total_active_ads_on_page).
minactiveads.notes: find_winning_products auto-applies minactiveads=50 for US when not set (see forced block).

minactiveadsgrowth.description: Minimum page active-ads percent growth over activeadsgrowthperiod.
minactiveadsgrowth.allowed_values: Human percent (25 = 25%); negatives allowed for decline.

activeadsgrowthperiod.description: Lookback window for active-ads growth filter.
activeadsgrowthperiod.allowed_values: 1w, 1m, 3m. Default 1m when min/max growth set. 1w=1 week, 1m=1 month, 3m=3 months.
activeadsgrowthperiod.notes: 14d/2m exist on the dashboard but are omitted from MCP — sparse wlads baselines return empty result sets.

minpagelikes.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. Ads missing the field excluded when min set.

minadspend.description: Minimum EU ad spend total in adspendtimeframe window.
minadspend.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier; can return upgrade JSON.

maxadspend.description: Maximum EU ad spend in window.
maxadspend.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. 999999 treated as no upper cap server-side.

adspendtimeframe.description: Rolling window ad spend is summed over (NOT a calendar month filter).

minreach.description: Minimum EU reach/views total in reachtimeframe window.
minreach.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier.

reachtimeframe.description: Rolling window reach is summed over.

mintraffic.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier.

minproductsonstore.description: Minimum published products on the Shopify store.

minprice.description: Minimum product price on landing page.

mincopylength.description: Minimum ad primary text character length.

minvideolength.description: Minimum video duration in seconds (use with mediafilter=videos).

mindays.description: Minimum days the ad has been running.
mindays.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier.

from.description: Ad launch date lower bound (Meta started field — when ad began running, NOT scrape date).
from.allowed_values: YYYY-MM-DD. Requires to on same range.

to.notes: To isolate ads running in a calendar month: ad_created_to=last day of month AND fromlastseen=first day of month.

product_from.description: Shopify product creation date lower bound.

pagefrom.description: Facebook page creation date lower bound.

activestatus.description: Legacy dashboard param (no longer applied to ES queries).
activestatus.allowed_values: Ignored — use adstatus or last_seen_from/to instead.

adstatus.description: Dashboard Status filter — recently seen vs stale ads.
adstatus.allowed_values: active (lastSeen or updated_at within last 4 days), inactive (neither field within last 4 days), All/empty (no status filter).
adstatus.notes: find_winning_products forces active. Same as dashboard Status = Active.

sorting.allowed_values: relevance, datefound, mostrecent, lastseen, adspend, longestrunning, reach, adsetamount, consistency, monthlyvisits, monthlytraffic, monthlyrevenue, pageactiveads, toprank, mostsaved. Aliases: rank/top_ad/best_ranked→toprank (asc = best rank first, desc = worst rank first). ad_started→mostrecent. monthly_visits→monthlyvisits. monthly_traffic→monthlytraffic.

page.description: Pagination page index (informational). Deep pagination requires scroll from the previous response — incrementing page alone does not advance the result set.
page.allowed_values: MCP uses 1-based page (1=first page); echoed value is 0-based internal page sent to API.

scroll.description: Opaque pagination cursor. Empty/omit on the first request; pass the response scroll value on the next request with the same filters to fetch more ads. Required to download beyond the first page (especially sort_by=lastseen).
scroll.allowed_values: Opaque string from previous response; empty string or omit for first page. Stop when scroll is null/absent or data is shorter than a full page.
